`using` declares a resource that is disposed automatically when the scope exits, even on an exception: the object needs a [Symbol.dispose]() method (or Symbol.asyncDispose with `await using`), and several are disposed in reverse order. It's like try/finally without writing it. The catch is the runtime: it needs Symbol.dispose to exist or a polyfill, and the right lib/target settings in tsconfig. Action: none unless you want a small example in scripts/; I'd check our runtime and tsconfig before using it anywhere real.

tsx uses esbuild to strip types and run the file, so it doesn't type-check and starts almost instantly, with ESM and CommonJS working without setup. ts-node uses the real TypeScript compiler by default, so it type-checks while running but starts slower and has fiddlier ESM support. Use tsx for running scripts and keep `tsc --noEmit` for type checking. They're different. HTTP/1.1 keep-alive only reuses a TCP connection for the next request, but each connection carries one request at a time, so browsers open several in parallel and still queue behind slow responses. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests and responses as interleaved streams on a single connection, with header compression as well. Action: none; I can sketch a quick diagram if it helps in standup.

A Deployment treats pods as interchangeable: any pod can be replaced or scaled freely, with no stable identity or per-pod storage. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable name, stable network identity and its own persistent volume, and starts and stops them in order. Pick it for databases, brokers or anything that needs per-instance storage or identity. Action: none.
